strengths: Novel and conceptually compelling formulation: The paper shifts the focus of cognitive state decoding from coarse procedural task classification (e.g., normal reading vs. annotation) to fine-grained, text-specific semantic goal decoding.

Methodological rigor: The experimental design is thorough, employing strict article-level cross-validation splits to test generalization across new readers, new texts, and both, alongside linear mixed-effects models for statistical significance testing.

Comprehensive evaluation framework: The authors evaluate both discriminative selection (with fine-grained sub-evaluations on different vs. shared critical text spans) and generative reconstruction across multiple surface, semantic, and downstream task metrics (e.g., question word agreement, taxonomy classification, and QA answering consistency).

Strong discriminative results: RoBERTEye-Fixations achieves clear and statistically significant gains over baselines, notably outperforming chance even when distinguishing between two questions targeting the exact same critical span in the text.
weaknesses: Limited generative generalization to unseen texts: While DalEye-Llama demonstrates promising reconstruction results in the 'New Participant' regime, performance degrades substantially on 'New Text' and 'New Text & Participant' regimes, where it often falls below or parity with simple heuristic baselines (such as incorrect human questions targeting the critical span or text-only arbitrary questions).

Restricted dataset scale and diversity: The study relies on 162 paragraphs and 486 questions from the OneStopQA dataset. While large for lab-grade eye-tracking standards, this limited textual diversity restricts the capacity of decoder LLMs to generalize their goal inference capabilities.
Minor presentation omission: In Section 10 (Reproducibility Statement), the URL reference for the OneStop dataset repository appears to have been omitted ('publicly available at').

strengths: Novel and compelling task formulation: while previous work primarily addressed procedural task classification (e.g., ordinary reading vs. skimming or annotation), this paper takes a significant step forward by tackling semantic, text-specific information-seeking goal decoding in both discriminative selection and open-ended generative reconstruction setups.

Methodological rigor: the experimental design is thorough, using a 10-fold cross-validation scheme partitioned into New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant splits to evaluate generalization, accompanied by linear mixed-effects models for rigorous statistical significance testing.

Comprehensive model exploration: the authors adapt existing discriminative gaze-text architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye) and introduce novel generative multimodal LLM formulations (both prompt-based Llama fine-tuning and multimodal LLaVA adaptation).

Creative evaluation protocol for generation: evaluating open-ended reconstruction using semantic category alignment, question word identification, and particularly downstream QA accuracy via a RACE-finetuned reader provides informative insights into whether reconstructed questions preserve functional semantic intent.
Paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and transparent about limitations and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: Generalization gap on unseen texts: For the generative reconstruction task (DalEye-Llama), model performance degrades substantially in the New Item / New Text regime (e.g., Question Word Kappa drops from 0.478 to 0.069, and QA accuracy drops below the 'incorrect human question - same critical span' baseline). This indicates that the generative model relies heavily on memorized text-question pairings rather than reliably decoding novel goals from gaze alone.

Lack of analysis for DalEye-LLaVA failure: DalEye-LLaVA performs near chance level across almost all settings (33.5% All selection accuracy vs. 33.0% chance). A deeper ablation or qualitative error analysis explaining why continuous fixation embeddings failed in comparison to textual serialization (DalEye-Llama) would strengthen the modeling contributions.

Dataset scale constraint: Although OneStop contains over 1M word tokens of gaze data, it comprises only 162 unique paragraphs and 486 questions, which restricts the diversity of semantic goals available for training large generative models.

strengths: Novel and scientifically compelling task formulation: moving beyond procedural task classification (e.g., normal reading vs. skimming) to decoding semantic, content-specific information-seeking goals directly from reader eye movements.

Rigorous experimental design and data splitting: the authors evaluate generalization across three distinct regimes (New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant) and use linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts/slopes to properly account for repeated-measures non-independence.

Comprehensive exploration of modeling paradigms: benchmarks range from intuitive reading-time heuristic baselines to adapted discriminative architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye) and generative LLM approaches (DalEye-LLaVA and textualized DalEye-Llama).

Thorough evaluation of the generative reconstruction task: combining n-gram overlap (BLEU), semantic embeddings (BERTScore), categorical alignment (question word, UIUC category), and downstream functional validity (downstream QA task accuracy).
weaknesses: Limited generalization in open-ended question reconstruction on unseen texts: in the New Text and New Text & Participant regimes, reconstruction performance drops sharply (e.g., question word Kappa drops from 0.478 to 0.069), indicating that the generative model struggles to decode arbitrary questions without having observed the text during training.

Relatively constrained dataset scale: the OneStop dataset comprises 162 paragraphs and 486 questions. While extensive in terms of eye-tracking fixations (~1M tokens), the textual diversity is small for training modern multimodal LLMs, likely exacerbating text-level overfitting.

Underperformance of the multimodal vision-language architecture (DalEye-LLaVA): the model fails to significantly outperform chance on 3-way selection (33.5% vs. 33.0%), showing that the proposed continuous fixation encoder struggles to transfer effectively within this multimodal framework.

strengths: Novel and conceptually significant problem: Formulating the task of decoding specific, semantic information-seeking goals (reading questions) directly from human eye movement scanpaths over text, moving beyond coarse procedural reading state classification.

Methodological rigor and experimental setup: The paper establishes a 10-fold cross-validation scheme carefully partitioned into New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant splits to evaluate out-of-distribution generalization without data leakage. The use of linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts/slopes properly handles the non-i.i.d. structure of eye-tracking data.

Comprehensive modeling and evaluation: The study covers both discriminative goal selection and generative goal reconstruction. Evaluates multiple architectures (similarity heuristics, Haller RNN, RoBERTEye, LoRA-finetuned LLaMA-3.1, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini zero/few-shot) against text-only baselines and human foils.

Insightful cognitive analysis: The authors link model predictions to cognitive indicators of reading behavior via mixed-effects modeling, demonstrating that model performance correlates with gaze efficiency (longer dwell times inside the critical span vs. shorter dwell times outside), providing valuable convergence with psycholinguistic theory.
weaknesses: Limited dataset and text domain diversity: The evaluation relies exclusively on the OneStopQA reading corpus (Guardian news articles at paragraph level, ~100 words). It remains an open question how well these findings generalize to longer, multi-paragraph documents, technical texts, or natural web browsing environments.

Drop in generative reconstruction on novel texts: In the New Text and New Text & Participant regimes, the performance gap between gaze-augmented generative models and text-only baselines diminishes substantially, with some metrics showing parity with text-only generation. While expected given the difficulty of the task, it underscores the current limitations of free-form goal generation on unseen contexts.

Limited success of learned continuous multimodal encoders: The continuous eye-movement encoder (DalEye-LLaVA) struggled compared to prompt-based textual serialization (DalEye-Llama). While reporting negative results is commendable, a deeper diagnostic analysis of why continuous scanpath embeddings failed would provide stronger architectural guidance for multimodal gaze modeling.

strengths: Pioneering and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper transitions from prior coarse, procedural reading task classification (e.g., reading vs. skimming) to fine-grained, semantic goal decoding—inferring or reconstructing the specific question motivating the reader.

Rigorous experimental methodology: The paper carefully accounts for the non-i.i.d. structure of eye-tracking data by evaluating across three distinct generalization splits (New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant) and using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes for sound statistical testing.

Comprehensive exploration of both discriminative and generative paradigms: The work covers competitive baselines, adapted discriminative neural sequence models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye), fine-tuned open/closed LLMs (DalEye-Llama, DalEye-GPT), and frontier zero/few-shot prompting.

Strong cognitive interpretability: The analysis linking RoBERTEye performance to trial- and reader-level features (e.g., reading time ratio inside vs. outside the critical span) grounds the deep learning results directly in psycholinguistic theory.
Thorough supplementary studies: The appendix provides valuable analyses, including fixation vs. word-level representation ablations, prompt sensitivity studies, and n-gram overlap characterization.
weaknesses: Data source limitation: Experiments are conducted exclusively on a single eye-tracking dataset (OneStop, 162 paragraphs and 486 questions). While sizable for laboratory eye-tracking benchmarks, it represents a relatively narrow domain (news articles), leaving open how well findings translate to longer multi-paragraph documents, technical texts, or naturalistic web browsing.

Substantial generalization drop in open-ended generation on unseen texts: In the New Text condition, generative performance drops markedly (e.g., BLEU dropping from ~0.55 down to ~0.25), where models often perform close to or below human same-span baseline heuristics, underscoring the extreme difficulty of zero-shot goal reconstruction on novel content.

Limited success of end-to-end multimodal gaze architectures: The proposed continuous embedding-based multimodal model (DalEye-LLaVA) underperformed the simpler textual serialization of fixations, leaving optimal continuous feature fusion for gaze-to-text generation as an unresolved open question.

Constrained candidate set for selection: The discriminative goal selection task is evaluated on 3 candidate questions per text, which is relatively small compared to practical open-world retrieval scenarios.

strengths: Novel and compelling task formulation: While prior work on cognitive state decoding has largely focused on coarse procedural distinctions (e.g., skim-reading vs. comprehension), this paper pioneers fine-grained semantic goal decoding—both discriminatively selecting and generatively reconstructing text-specific reading goals from gaze trajectories.

Methodological and statistical rigor: The authors employ 10-fold cross-validation partitioned strictly at the article and participant level (evaluating New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant regimes). Furthermore, all statistical significance tests are properly conducted using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes to account for the repeated-measures structure of eye-tracking data.

Comprehensive baseline comparisons and ablations: The evaluation thoroughly benchmarks against text-only LLMs (finetuned identically without gaze), human alternative questions, and heuristic baselines, confirming that models are genuinely leveraging gaze dynamics rather than text heuristics or pretraining memorization. The paper also includes insightful ablations over gaze features, prompts, and representation granularities.

Strong psycholinguistic grounding: The mixed-effects analysis linking RoBERTEye model accuracy to cognitive features (e.g., fixation time allocation inside vs. outside critical spans, trial progression, reading comprehension performance) provides valuable interpretability and grounds the machine learning findings in reading psychology theory.
weaknesses: Domain and dataset scope: Experiments are restricted to a single dataset (OneStop, comprising Guardian news paragraphs with three questions each). Evaluating across diverse genres (e.g., technical documentation, scientific texts) would provide stronger evidence of broader real-world applicability.

Performance bottleneck in generative reconstruction on novel texts: On the New Text regime, generative performance drops substantially, and metrics like BLEU and BERTScore fall behind or near the 'Incorrect Human (same critical span)' baseline, showing that zero-shot free-form goal reconstruction on completely unseen content remains challenging.

Hardware and practical deployment gap: The dataset relies on laboratory-grade eye trackers (EyeLink 1000 Plus). While the scientific proof of concept is clear, the downstream applications envisioned in the discussion (e.g., real-time web personalization, assistive tech) would likely face significant hurdles when applied to noisier, webcam-based gaze tracking.
